BOOK_B.title: Third party defendant's options

commentary.text: Rule 3.47 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.47. 1. Function of Rule … a plaintiff does have a right to move to set aside a third party notice. The express right given to a plaintiff by R. 68 may be in recognition of the fact that a third party becomes a de facto defendant for the purpose of disputing the defendant's liability to the plaintiff. That is, the third party can defend the plaintiff's claim against the defendant in addition to defending the defendant's claim against himself: R. 71(2). If a plaintiff can successfully have a third party notice set aside he eliminates a possible adversary in advancing his claim against the defendant. Westlands Industrial Park Ltd. v. Burgee Developments Ltd. (1982), 23 Alta. L.R. (2d) 201 at 203 (Master). 2. Application to Strike after Statement of Defence In my view, R. 68 does not preclude an application to strike a third party notice being made after a defence has been filed… The filing of a defence and the passage of time cannot legitimize a third party notice which has no foundation. Herr v. Herr (1991), 80 Alta. L.R. (2d) 328 (Q.B.) at 334, per O'Leary J. 3. Grounds for Setting Aside Rule 68 does not indicate on what grounds a third party notice can be set aside. However, as the rule deals with both a third party or a plaintiff moving to set aside the notice, logically a plaintiff should be able to rely at least on those grounds that a third party can rely on. Westlands Industrial Park Ltd. v. Burgee Developments Ltd. (1982), 23 Alta. L.R. (2d) 201 at 203 (Master). 4. If Third Party Notice Provides Full Defence to Defendant Both parties rely on Alberta Energy Co. v. Daniel Industries Inc. et al. (1990), 100 A.R. 74 (C.A.), as the leading case in this area. In Alberta Energy, supra, the Court of Appeal held that if the third party notice provides the defendant with a full answer to the plaintiff's claim, it should be struck. However, if it is possible that the third party and the defendant are jointly liable, the notice should stand. The court held at p. 75: The rule forbids a third party notice which is based solely on facts which, if proved, would give a complete defence to the main action. In such a case the very facts which would make the third party liable to the defendant would make the defendant not liable to the plaintiff. The main action would be dismissed, and there would be no need for contribution or indemnity. It is clear from Alberta Energy, supra, that if the allegations against the Crown provide an “all or nothing” answer to Burnco's [plaintiff's] claim, the third party notice is improper. Burnco Rock Products Ltd. v. Schomburg Industries (Canada) Inc. (1998), 229 A.R. 37 ((Q.B.)), at 40, per Moore C.J.Q.B. The Court of Appeal allowed an appeal from Chief Justice Moore's decision [(1998) 228 A.R. 163], but did not disagree with the above statement of law. 5. Practice of Court on Application … the court, in exercising its discretion under R. 68 of the Alberta Rules of Court, should examine the pleadings to determine whether there are common issues that might be decided differently if the indemnity proceedings were severed from the principal action. Schug v. Odegaard (1984), 32 Alta. L.R. (2d) 355 at 362 (Q.B.).
